facts.statement: Eostrix is an extinct genus of primitive owls belonging to the family Protostrigidae.
facts.quote: Eostrix is a genus of extinct primitive owls in the family Protostrigidae, along with Oligostrix and Minerva.

facts.statement: The genus Eostrix was established by Pierce Brodkorb in 1971 to reclassify the species formerly known as Protostrix mimica.
facts.quote: The genus was created by Pierce Brodkorb in 1971 to place a fossil species known until that time as Protostrix mimica.

facts.statement: Eostrix fossils date from the early Eocene and have been found in the United States, Europe, and Mongolia.
facts.quote: These owls date from the early Eocene of the United States, Europe, and Mongolia.

facts.statement: The species E. mimica was described by Alexander Wetmore in 1938 based on hindlimb elements found in Eocene strata in Wyoming.
facts.quote: E. mimica described in 1938 by Alexander Wetmore using hindlimb elements in Eocene strata in Wyoming.

facts.statement: The species E. martinellii was described in 1972 from a left tarsometatarsus found by Jorge Martinelli in 1970 in Fremont County, Wyoming.
facts.quote: E. martinellii was described in 1972 from a left tarsometatarsus (lower leg bone) recovered from an escarpment above the southeastern bank of Cottonwood Creek in Fremont County, Wyoming by Jorge Martinelli on a field trip in 1970 under the auspices of the University of Kansas.

facts.statement: The fossils of E. martinellii were recovered from the Lysite member of the Wind River Formation.
facts.quote: The strata was a Lysite member of the Wind River Formation.

facts.statement: E. martinellii was the smaller of the two species and was similar in size to the modern long-eared owl.
facts.quote: The smaller of the two species, it was similar in size to the living long-eared owl (Asio otus).

facts.statement: E. martinellii is distinguished from living owls by unique grooves on its tarsometatarsus, including a groove for digit 2, a deep posterior groove for digit 3, and a rounded trochlea for digit 4.
facts.quote: Differences in the trochleas (grooves) of the lower end of the tarsometatarsus set it apart from living owls, namely a groove in the trochlea for digit 2, a deeper posterior groove in a relatively narrow trochlea for digit 3, and an unusually rounded trochlea for digit 4.

facts.statement: The species E. vincenti was described by Colin Harrison in 1980 from early Eocene London Clay in England.
facts.quote: E. vincenti described in 1980 by Colin Harrison from the early Eocene London Clay in England, known from pedal phalanx and proximal tarsometatarsus bones.

facts.statement: Some scholars debate whether E. vincenti belongs in the genus Eostrix or resembles the genus Necrobyas more closely.
facts.quote: Some scholars think E. vincenti resembles Necrobyas more than Eostrix.

facts.statement: The species E. tsaganica was described in 2011 by Evgeny Kurochkin and Gareth J. Dyke from fossils found in Mongolia.
facts.quote: E. tsaganica described in 2011 by Evgeny Kurochkin and Gareth J. Dyke, found in Mongolia.

facts.statement: Gerald Mayr described the species E. gulottai in 2016 from the early Eocene Nanjemoy Formation in Virginia.
facts.quote: In 2016, Gerald Mayr described E. gulottai from the early Eocene Nanjemoy Formation in Virginia.

facts.statement: In 2022, Mayr and Kitchener reclassified E. gulottai into the genus Ypresiglaux, changing its name to Y. gulottai.
facts.quote: However, in 2022, Mayr, alongside Andrew C. Kitchener, moved 'E.' gulottai to the genus Ypresiglaux as the new combination Y. gulottai.

facts.statement: Eostrix is classified within the family Protostrigidae.
Eostrix lived during the Ypresian stage, between 56 and 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)
